name: func_801681A0
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Draws the password screen's selection frame around the record pointed to by the first argument into the ordering table in the second. It builds two primitives in the PS1 scratchpad - a five-word three-vertex polyline at 0x1F800000 with code 0x48 and a four-word two-vertex line at 0x1F800040 with code 0x50 - and submits each through func_8005B260 eight times with priority from the record's s16 at +0x14 masked to 16 bits and otag 1. The record's geometry is x at +0x30 y at +0x32 width at +0x3C and height at +0x3E all halfwords. Four submissions draw corner brackets one per corner: the top left runs from x minus 1 and y plus 3 up to x minus 1 and y minus 1 then right to x plus 3; the other three mirror it about x plus width and y plus height. Four more draw lines from the frame out to the screen edges - up from the top centre to y zero down from the bottom centre to y 192 left from the left centre to x zero and right from the right centre to x 320 - which is the callout that ties the frame to whatever is off-screen. Both primitives take colour 0x0000FF00 written as one word at +4 before the length and code bytes overwrite +3 and +7 and the polyline takes a second colour word 0x55555555 at +0x14. Builds 150 instructions against 147. Lever found: the width and height locals must be unsigned. As s32 the halving for the two centre lines emits srav where the target has srlv - GCC cannot prove a value loaded with lhu into a signed local is non-negative. Measured and not helping: a u16 local for the x plus 3 corner value which the target spills with sw and reloads with lhu. What remains is three instructions of register pressure - the target keeps x in a callee-saved register and adds 2 in place for the last line while the build spills the sum through the stack. Reconstructed independently and three findings correct or sharpen the note above. First a semantic correction: the four callout lines are symmetric and all start two pixels inside the frame, so the bottom line begins at y plus height minus 2 rather than minus 1, matching the top at y plus 2, the left at x plus 2 and the right at x plus width minus 2. Second, the priority is not masked in the source at all. Writing pri equals the s16 at plus 0x14 and 0xFFFF folds the lh and the andi into a single lhu, which is why the mask looked like it belonged to the load; the target's lh followed by a distant andi is what a u16 third parameter on func_8005B260 produces, with the conversion done once at the first call site and reused. That alone took the candidate from 124 differing positions to 88. Third, the target updates two values in place rather than recomputing them: x plus equals 2 before the left line, and the bottom local minus equals 2 before the bottom line, where the bottom local already holds y plus height from the third corner. The residual is now exact and is three instructions in one place. The target keeps x in callee-saved s6 and spends one addiu s6 s6 2; the build spills x and spends lw, addiu, sw and lhu. The competing value is the x plus 3 corner, which the target parks in a stack slot with sw and reloads with lhu. Re-measured against this corrected shape and still inert: declaring the x plus 3 local u16 does not make GCC spill it, and spelling x plus 3 inline at both corners does not free the register either because GCC re-forms the common subexpression. So the open question is only which of the two values the allocator spills. Correction to the reading above, which created a false lead. The sw followed by lhu on the spilled x plus 3 corner is not a type tell and does not mean the source declares that value u16. Rebuilding this candidate and looking at its own output shows the identical idiom on the spilled x, which is a plain s32 local: sw to the slot, then lw when the value feeds arithmetic and lhu when it feeds a halfword store. The reload width follows the use, not the declaration, so the pair says nothing about the declared type and only says the value is in a stack slot. Both builds therefore spend the same idiom on whichever value loses the register; the whole residual is which one that is. By use count x should win as it does in the target - it feeds x minus 1, x plus 3, x plus width, the centre sum and x plus 2, five uses against the corner value's two. Measured against this shape and not helping: declaring the corner value u16, re-confirmed; and assigning x plus 2 to a separate local instead of updating x in place, which leaves both the count and the positions unchanged, so the in-place update is not what costs x its register. The residual is not a two-way contest between x and the x plus 3 corner, and reading it that way has been sending attempts at the wrong question. Read off the target directly: it uses all nine callee-saved registers and spills three values to the frame, not one. s0 and s1 hold the two scratchpad primitives, s8 the ordering table, s4 the priority already converted to 16 bits, s5 y, s6 x, s2 the width, s3 y plus height, and s7 x minus 1. The frame holds the height at 16(sp), stored immediately after it is loaded and before any call and reloaded twice, x plus 3 at 20(sp), and x plus width at 24(sp). So the target keeps x and spills three separate values, and the question is not which of two loses a register. Two asymmetries in that assignment are the actual leads. First, x minus 1 has its own callee-saved register: it is computed once at instruction 40 and read at both left corners, 43 and 44 for the top and 82 and 83 for the bottom, so the source names it as a local rather than recomputing it per corner. Any candidate that spells x minus 1 at each corner is competing for a different set of registers than the target and should not be expected to match. Second, the two dimensions are treated oppositely although they are written the same way: the width lives in s2 for the whole function while the height is spilled the moment it is loaded, and correspondingly y plus height keeps s3 while x plus width is spilled. So whatever distinguishes them is between the width and the height, not between x and its corner. Both of those are checkable against a rebuilt candidate and neither has been tried. Rebuilt from the corrected reading and it now builds 148 against 147, one over rather than three, with 139 differing positions. The shape that gets there writes only the fields that change at each submission rather than all six: the first corner sets both x fields to x minus 1, both upper y fields to y minus 1 and the lower to y plus 3 and the third x to x plus 3; the second changes only the three x fields to x plus width plus 1 and x plus width minus 3; the third changes only the three y fields against y plus height; and the fourth changes only the x fields back. The four callouts likewise touch only what moves. Both x and y are updated in place at the end, x plus equals 2 and y plus equals height over two, and the width local is overwritten by x plus width over two, which is why the width can share a register with that centre and the height cannot. The residual reframes again and the new reading is checkable. Side by side the target holds the priority, y, x, x minus 1 and the ordering table in s4 to s8 and spills the height, x plus 3 and x plus width; the candidate holds the priority, y, x plus 3, x minus 1 and the width, and spills x, the height and the ordering table. The candidate never gives the ordering table a register at all: it stores the incoming argument to the frame at instruction 20 and reloads it before every one of the eight calls, where the target copies it to s8 at instruction 3 and never touches memory. That is the root difference rather than the x contest, because a spilled ordering table frees exactly the register that then goes to x plus 3. So the question to answer next is why the second parameter loses its register, not which of x and its corner wins one. Re-measured against this corrected shape: spelling x plus 3 inline at both corners instead of naming it is byte-identical, so the recorded note that the compiler re-forms that common subexpression holds here too and that avenue stays closed. Correction to the previous entry: the spilled ordering table is not what costs the extra instruction. Each reload of it replaces one move from a callee-saved register one for one, eight sites either way, so the spill is count-neutral and only changes which registers hold what. The single extra instruction is x. The target updates it in place with one addiu s6 s6 2 before the left callout, while the candidate has x in a frame slot and spends lw, addiu and sw there. So the whole residual is that one update, and the question is only whether x holds a register at that point. Three things were measured against the rebuilt candidate and none of them moves it. Copying the ordering-table parameter into a local before the first call is coalesced away and gives byte-identical output. Writing the fourth corner's x as x minus 1 plus 4 rather than x plus 3, so that it derives from a value already in a register instead of forming the same common subexpression, is also byte-identical, which strengthens the recorded finding that this expression cannot be kept out of its own register by how it is spelled. Both candidates spill exactly three values, so this is a preference rather than a pressure problem. One further difference is real but count-neutral and worth recording so it is not mistaken for a lead: both halvings in the target are srlv against the register that holds the calls' fourth argument, the constant 1, where the candidate emits an immediate srl. The target is reusing the argument constant as the shift amount, which means that constant is a shared pseudo across the whole function rather than eight separate literals. Reconstructed from this note and stored in notes/overlays/candidates.md, re-verified from the stored copy, so continuing does not start with a rebuild. Triaging it by opcode multiset rather than by position count located the remaining work precisely and cheaply. The first build read 149 instructions, 131 differing positions and an opcode distance of 10, made up of two srl where the target has srlv, one missing andi, one missing lhu, and three extra lw with one extra sw. Declaring the third parameter of func_8005B260 as u16 rather than s32 supplies the missing andi, which confirms the recorded reading that the priority mask is a parameter conversion rather than a mask in the source; it takes the distance to 9 and the differing positions from 131 to 109, at the cost of one instruction, 150 against 149. The stored candidate is the u16 shape on the reasoning that the multiset is the better guide. What is left in the mix is two srl against the target's srlv, and the lhu with the lw and sw around the spilled x plus 3 corner. The srlv pair is the target shifting by the register that already holds the fourth argument's 1; naming a local for that 1 and passing it to all eight calls does not reproduce it, because the compiler folds the constant back into the shifts. Jump counts agree at zero for both, so block placement is not involved. Four axes are now closed against the opcode distance rather than against the position count, and the distance stays at 9 through all of them. The named local for the fourth argument's 1 is inert and has been removed from the stored candidate: passing a literal 1 and shifting by a literal 1 gives byte-identical output, so the local suggested a lever that is not there. That also means the earlier improvement came entirely from the u16 third parameter and not from the shift spelling. Declaring that local volatile is much worse, 154 instructions and distance 23. Assigning it immediately before each shift, and routing the shift through a second local copied from it, are both inert. Removing the x minus 1 local and spelling it inline is inert. Declaring the x plus 3 corner u16, and declaring both it and the right edge u16, are inert, which confirms the earlier recorded negative with a better instrument. On the profile axis gcc_2_8_1_g8_split, gcc_2_8_1_cc_g0_as_g8_split and gcc_2_8_1_g0_keep_large_ori are all identical to the default at distance 9, and only the scheduling variants move it, both for the worse at 28 and 18. So the remaining mix difference, two srl against srlv and the lhu with the lw and sw around the spill, is not reachable from the source spellings tried so far or from the profile. The srlv question is now understood rather than merely observed, and the note above is wrong on one point: it is not true that every spelling of the 1 folds. A plain local does fold and is inert, as recorded. A local read from a volatile does not fold and produces srlv twice, exactly the target's form, and a static or extern global does the same. So srlv is reachable; what is not reachable so far is reaching it for free. Measured: the literal builds 150 at distance 9 with srl twice; the volatile-sourced local builds 155 at distance 22 with srlv twice; a static or extern global builds 157 at distance 44 with srlv twice. Every spelling that buys the right shift form pays more elsewhere than the two positions it wins, so none of them should be adopted. What this establishes is the mechanism. srlv requires a shift amount the compiler cannot prove constant, so in the original source the 1 is a variable and not a literal. The disassembly supports that independently and more strongly than the shifts alone do: the target keeps 1 in a3 and uses it as a general operand, not only as the fourth argument of the four calls to 0x5B260 and as the shift amount at 92 and 117, but as an ordinary addend at 59, where it computes addu v0,t0,a3 rather than addiu v0,t0,1. A literal would never produce that. So the remaining work on this function is to find what that variable is in game terms - something whose value happens to be 1 and which the compiler cannot fold, rather than another way of writing the constant. Trying further spellings of a literal 1 is closed; three have now been measured and the two that work are both too expensive. The addition axis is measured and closed, and it was genuinely untried. This row and its predecessors varied the 1 at the call arguments and at the two shifts, but never at the four additions, even though the target's clearest evidence that the 1 lives in a register is an addition rather than a shift: addu v0,t0,a3 at index 59. All eight combinations of routing the additions, the arguments and the shifts through a single local assigned once at the top were built against every profile, 232 cells. Every one is equal to or worse than the literal baseline at distance 9, because the compiler folds the local at all three kinds of use. That strengthens rather than weakens the recorded conclusion: only a value the compiler cannot prove constant reaches srlv, and every such spelling costs more than the two positions it wins. The remaining opcode distance is now decoded rather than described, and the axis that looked most promising is closed with evidence. Against the stored candidate the class-level multiset difference is exactly: two srl where the target has srlv, three extra lw and one extra sw against one missing lhu. The second group is one extra live value - this build spills three values where the target spills two, keeping x+3 in s7 while the target spills it and reloads it twice as a halfword, which is where the lhu goes. The first group is the real blocker. The target shifts by a3, the register holding the fourth argument's 1, at both halvings. A register-form shift needs a non-constant count in the RTL, and an isolating probe settles where one can come from: of four small functions that pass 1 as a call argument and halve a value, only the one taking the count as a function parameter emits the register form; a literal, a local assigned 1, and a halving hoisted above the call all emit srl by immediate. Scaled up to this function the same holds - a local used as the fourth argument of all eight calls and as both shift counts, ten uses in total, is still folded to the immediate. The parameter route is closed separately by the call convention: func_801681A0 is not called directly but installed as a hook at obj+0x4C by NameEntry_Init, and the other matched hook at that slot, func_80016D04, takes exactly two arguments, so there is no third or fourth parameter to carry a count. Measured anyway and much worse: a third parameter builds 148 at distance 29 and a fourth builds the target's 147 but at distance 28, spilling thirteen extra loads. Also measured and inert or worse this pass: w and h as u32, s32, u16 and s16 in all sixteen combinations; the halving as a shift, a divide, inlined into the store, or through a named local; the halvings computed before the calls instead of after; x-1 and x+3 recomputed instead of cached, which is byte-identical because the compiler rediscovers them; x+w and y+h inlined instead of cached; and all twenty-nine profiles, where nothing beats gcc_2_8_1_g0_split's 150 at distance 9. The conclusion to carry forward is that the halving cannot be spelled as a shift by a compile-time 1 at all, so either the value being halved or the count reaches this function by a route the current reconstruction does not have. Matched with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. Four findings, and the first one overturns the conclusion this row carried for several passes. The two halvings reach srlv from a compile-time 1 after all: inlining x + (w >> 1) into the two stores that use it, instead of assigning it to a local first, emits the register form, because the expression is then evaluated where the argument register already holds 1 and CSE substitutes it. Doing that at one halving takes the distance from 9 to 7 and at both takes it to 5, and no volatile, global or extra parameter is needed. The earlier reading that a register-form shift proves a non-constant count does not apply here, and the supporting evidence for it was also wrong: the candidate reproduces addu v0,t0,a3 with a plain literal, because GCC reuses the argument register it has just loaded, so that instruction never showed the 1 was a variable. Second, the dimension types are a false lead that nearly became a wrong conclusion. Declaring the height u16 reaches the target's 147 instructions and looks decisive, but it carries an andi the target does not have, and once the load order below is right the original u32 for both width and height is correct and the u16 is worse. The matched source declares w and h exactly as the candidate always did. Third, the order of the five field loads decides which value the allocator spills. Sweeping all 120 permutations against the corrected shape reaches an exact instruction mix, and the winning order is pri, x, y, w, h. Fourth, the residual after that is statement order inside the blocks: the six stores of the first corner, 720 permutations, and the four stores of each centre line, 576 permutations for the pair. Nothing was found by sweeping an axis alone. Every one of the four had been measured before on an earlier base and recorded as inert or worse, and each became decisive only once an earlier one was in place; the final match came out of a 2880-cell product of the load order against the last block's store order, where the best load order alone and the best store order alone were both different from the pair that matches.

name: NameEntry_Init

It starts the 0x7010 track through func_8003FF08 resets the display through func_800403F0 clears the three state bytes at D_8016D400 D_8016D403 and D_8016D408 and publishes gSaveData_aPlayerNameSjis into D_8016D418 before loading it with func_8003BC40 from D_801B125A with six entries. It then places two backdrop sprites through func_8003B6AC and func_80035BE4 - one at 254 by 112 sized 204 by 96 with palette 16 and one at 243 by 262 sized 60 by 100 - and registers each with func_80039A14; the first also writes 16 into the two bytes at D_800EB0F8 plus 390 and 391 and registers the object 300 bytes into that block. func_80168138 is called with 2 and the same 2 is stored into D_8016D4D0. name: TextBox_GetGlyphAt
notes: Exact overlay match with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. Searches the node list at entry+0x24 of the 100-byte record for a node whose x at +0xC and y at +0xE match the arguments; the walk stops when bit 0x80 of the byte at +0x11 is clear and returns the node or zero. Nodes are 0x1C bytes. Three levers: the table base goes in its own local because writing base + index * 100 + 0x24 folds 0x24 into the %lo; the loop is for(;;) with explicit returns because while (flags & 0x80) lets GCC peel the first test and rotate; and the flags exit returns inline rather than breaking to a shared trailing return which costs the exiting branch its delay slot. The induction-variable blocker recorded earlier was a symptom of the rotation rather than a separate problem: the peeled load gave GCC +0x11 to build the combined giv from instead of the target's +0xE and the negative offsets followed from that.

name: func_80168AB4
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Password widget slide, the same 8.8 fixed point shape as FreeDuel_UpdateCursorTween. Bit 0x80 of the state byte at +0x6C marks the slide already primed: the first pass sets it calls func_800429D8 and divides the distance from the current pair at +0x30 and +0x32 to the target pair at +0x44 and +0x46 shifted left 8 by the frame count at +0x60 into the per-frame steps at +0x36 and +0x38. Bit 0x40 means the widget is retiring - each frame decrements +0x60 and at zero or below releases it through func_8004036C. Otherwise it advances through func_80042A78 and decrements +0x60; while that stays positive it spawns a trail sprite through func_8004002C and func_800400AC with func_80040510 at the widget's current position size 16 by 16 using the bytes at +0x5C +0x5D and +0x66 and the halfwords at +0x40 and +0x42 then sets its colour word to 0x606060 its timer to 6 its hook to func_80042BC0 and or-s 0x50000000 into its flags. At zero it sets bit 0x40 snaps the position pair to the target as one 32-bit word rearms +0x60 to 2 and asks TextBox_GetGlyphAt for node 3 at D_8016D42C shifted left 4; a non-null node is handed to func_80168CDC with 3 and the result gets hook func_801688AC and state 5. Matched with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. The rearm of +0x60 to 2 is written inside the third argument of the TextBox_GetGlyphAt call rather than as the statement before it. Everything else was already exact: 138 of 138 instructions at opcode distance 0, the entire residual a rotation of the closing block, with the target opening it on the move of zero into a2 and closing on the store of 2 while the build did the reverse and the seven instructions between them agreed. About 10,800 cells were measured against that rotation before it fell - every order of the three snap stores, every combination of splitting the three read-modify-writes, volatile and aliased-pointer spellings of the store, naming each argument in a local, every declaration order of the locals, and all twenty-nine profiles - and every one returned the same ten positions. They had to. A statement is emitted ahead of every argument, so no statement-level spelling changes where the store sits relative to the argument setup, and that position is the only thing deciding the rotation: the store and the zero for a2 are both ready at the same point with the same priority, so the scheduler breaks the tie on emission order. Carried inside the third argument the store is emitted after a1 is computed, its two instructions fall to the end of the block, and the move of zero into a2 takes the head. The wider lesson is that this note previously concluded the residual was not reachable from source and that the function should be left alone. That verdict was wrong, and it was wrong in a specific way worth remembering: a very large negative result measures the axes you thought of, and the count of cells says nothing about the ones you did not. Also checked and not applicable: the symbol-versus-literal address distinction worth five on func_80169734, since this function forms no addresses from integer casts.

name: func_80168CDC
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. The data-placement blocker recorded here is obsolete: the module_header carve has since happened, and 0x4 to 0x90 is now its own module_rodata subsegment rather than part of module_header. This is an ordinary conversion. This is the password screen's character to tile mapper. It takes a slot index and a widget pointer, indexes D_800EB0F8 with a stride of 100 bytes, reads the Shift-JIS code from the widget and turns it into a u and v pair plus a palette for func_80040510, drawing at the widget's x and y from +0xC and +0xE with a signed shift applied to x. A null widget takes a separate path that draws a fixed 0x80 by 0x80 tile at the coordinates held in the object at D_8016D404. The code path itself is ordinary: a four case switch remapping 0x8171 and 0x8173 to 0x8183 and 0x8172 and 0x8174 to 0x8184, compiled as a balanced comparison tree pivoting on 0x8172; then an unsigned range test for 0x824F to 0x829A which is the fullwidth digits and letters, with the two gaps 0x8259 to 0x825F and 0x827A to 0x8280 rejected, and the cell computed as column of the low nibble times 16 and row of the code minus 0x8240 shifted down and back up by 4 plus 0x48; and otherwise a linear search of a symbol table, where the matched index is itself the position, and a few special cases. Matched with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split. The symbol table is a flat s32 tbl[30], a non-static local array with an initialiser, terminated by -1; reading its 120 bytes as code and position pairs leaves every second halfword zero. Three declarations carry the match and each was found by asking what type produces the instruction rather than by trying spellings. The x nudge is s16, not s32 with an (s16) cast: its only values are 0 and plus or minus two, so combine proves a cast on an s32 redundant and deletes the widening altogether, while a declared s16 keeps it, and the widening is then emitted as a pair of shifts whose count CSE satisfies from a3, the register already holding the sprite width for argument 4. That is why the target has sllv and srav rather than sll and sra, and why an explicit shift pair through a local needed a seventh materialisation of 16 that the target does not have. The u and v texture origin are u8, so they are passed unmasked; any wider type needs an explicit and 0xff, and at s16 the compiler narrows that mask to 0xf0 and 0xf8 because it can prove the values are multiples of 16 and 8. The two rejected gaps share one body, written as a single or, which lets the compiler cross-jump them and lets reorg fill the range test's delay slot by copying the shared block's first instruction, which is the second move of zero the earlier candidates were missing. The table search compares code == tbl[i], with the code first. The route to the match is worth recording: the residual sat at opcode distance 2 for many passes, described as one extra addiu against one missing addu and attributed to a delay-slot fill choice. Both halves were real and independent, and both were reachable from declarations alone. What separated them was taking the multiset difference at the level of instruction classes rather than reading the position diff: the extra addiu and the missing addu cancelled in the layout, so the two columns stayed aligned and the position count showed one problem where there were two.

notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Mapped but not matched; a first-pass candidate builds 386 of 382 instructions, four over. Pre-flight is clean: no jump table, no frame pointer prologue and no frame-bound block copy, so unlike func_8016A37C and func_80168CDC this one is an ordinary candidate. It is the password keyboard's per-frame handler and it is the same family as FreeDuel_UpdateScreen. While bit 0x4000 of D_8016D4D4 is set the cursor widget in D_8016D404 is sliding: its +0x3C creeps two at a time toward the byte at +0x5E plus 16, func_80042A78 advances it, and when the counter at +0x60 reaches zero it snaps +0x3C to +0x5E plus 16, restores +0x30 and +0x32 from D_8016D434 and D_8016D436, clears the bit and falls through into input handling rather than returning. The d-pad bits of D_8009B3A4 move a column in D_8016D401 wrapping over 0 to 14 and a row in D_8016D402 wrapping over 0 to 8, except that a column of 11 or more clamps to 11 and takes the row from the two-entry table D_8016ABC0 indexed by the current row, which is how the right hand block moves vertically on its own. The chosen cell then comes from the keyboard grid D_8016AB38 which is fifteen wide; a negative entry means a continuation cell so the column walks by that signed amount until it lands on a real key, which is how multi-cell keys work. Bit 0x40 of the cell sets the widget's +0x5E to 0x14 and the low nibble becomes the row. The home position is then column times 20 plus 0x16, or plus 0x2A past column 11, and row times 18 plus 0x18, and the widget is given eight frames with 8.8 fixed point steps in +0x36 and +0x38. Select with bits 0xC0 of D_8009B394 reads the cell's low nibble: 4 calls NameEntry_AdjustLength, 6 sets bit 0x40 of D_8016D400 and submits two nodes, and anything else submits one node through TextBox_GetGlyphAt and func_80168CDC with hook func_80168708. Declarations that worked first time: D_8016AB38 as s8[][15] and D_8016ABC0 as u8[][2]. Lever found: the slide delta must name the intermediate, as home equals the widget's +0x3C minus 16 and then delta equals +0x5E minus home. Written as one expression GCC re-associates it to +0x5E plus 16 minus +0x3C and both the operand order and the register roles change. What remains is four instructions and a register assignment that starts at the widget pointer, which the target keeps in s1 and the candidate in s0. The register assignment recorded as the residual is read exactly and one cheap route to it is closed. The target loads D_8016D4D4 at index 2 and the widget pointer from D_8016D404 at index 5, both before the 0x4000 test at 13, keeps the widget in s1 for the whole function and gives s0 to the slide delta, whose live range is only indices 18 to 21. The obvious reading, that the widget simply has to be read before the test to win the earlier register, is wrong: an isolated probe of that opening reads the widget first and still puts it in s0 with the delta in s1, which is the candidate's assignment rather than the target's, and writing the two reads in either source order is byte-identical because the compiler schedules the state load first regardless. So the probe does not reproduce this function's allocation and this residual cannot be worked at probe cost the way func_8016A080's flag block can; it needs the full 382 instruction candidate and the pressure from s2 through s6, which are all live in the real function and absent from any probe of the opening. Decoded to instruction level, and five details are recorded here that the prose summary above does not carry and that a reconstruction would not guess. The per-frame steps are not a general fixed-point divide: the frame count is the constant 8, and the target emits ((target - current) << 8) / 8 as a signed shift with bias, addiu 7 then sra 3, at indices 200 to 216, so the source should divide by a literal 8 rather than by the widget's +0x60. The continuation walk is a do-while that re-reads the grid each turn and stores the column back to D_8016D401 inside the loop at 158, not a single correction. D_8016D402 is restored from D_8016D426 at 163 to 166 before the cell's low nibble overwrites it, so the row has two writers in that block. There is a whole input path the summary omits: bit 0x800 of D_8009B398 at 220 to 230 jumps the cursor straight to column 14 and row 8 and then rejoins the cell lookup at 137, which is also where the no-movement case lands, so index 137 is a three-way join and the sound at 47 is played on every one of them. And in the select branch the flag in s4 is used twice over, once as the first argument to both TextBox_GetGlyphAt and func_80168CDC and once as a variable shift amount, sllv s2 v0 s4 at 290, so the two node submissions differ only by that shift and the source almost certainly writes one call site with a 0-or-1 variable rather than two separate call sites. Block map for the rebuild: slide advance 15 to 32, slide snap 33 to 45, column movement 46 to 80, row movement and the right-hand-block table 81 to 132, cell lookup and continuation walk 137 to 174, home position 175 to 196, step setup 197 to 219, the 0x800 shortcut 220 to 230, and select from 231. Reconstructed from the block map above and reached 380 of 382 instructions, but only 85 of those positions match, so the count is nearly right while the basic-block layout is not. That distinction matters for the next attempt: the arithmetic and the call sequence are close to correct and should not be re-derived, but the if and else nesting places the select branch and the shared cell-lookup join in a different order from the target. The staged counts are worth keeping as a guide to how much each part is worth: the slide, movement, cell lookup, home position and step setup alone build 259, adding the select branch's first node submission takes it to 341, and adding the kind-equals-one tail with the D_8016D418 slot write takes it to 380. Two source shapes were measured on the nibble-4 arm. Writing it as one NameEntry_AdjustLength call site with the direction computed as 1 or -1, which is what the target has at 259 to 266, is byte-identical to writing two call sites in two arms, because the compiler merges them anyway, so that is not the lever it looks like. Giving that arm an early return builds 372, eight short, which confirms the nibble-4 path falls through into the common node submission at 291 rather than returning. The remaining work is layout rather than semantics. The 380 of 382 candidate is now stored in notes/overlays/candidates.md and re-verified from the stored copy, so continuing this function no longer starts with a rebuild. The layout residual is also located exactly: instructions 0 to 54 already agree, and the first real difference is at 56, where the target fills the delay slot of the 0x2000 branch with the lui for D_8016D401 while the build emits a nop. That single unfilled slot shifts everything after it and accounts for most of the 332 differing positions, so the count of differing positions overstates how much is actually wrong. Measured against it and not helping: reading the column into a local at the top of the movement block, which builds 375; addressing the column through a named pointer taken at the top of the function, which builds 381 but with 348 positions; and the profile axis, where gcc_2_8_1_cc_g0_as_g8_split is identical to the default and no_sched1, no_sched2_split and g8_split build 387, 377 and 362 with more differing positions each. The jump-count lever recorded for func_80046294 applies here and gives a sharper diagnostic than the differing-position count. The target has nine unconditional jumps and the stored candidate has eleven, so two blocks are placed wrongly rather than compiled wrongly. Acting on it helped once: writing the D_8016D426 store into each of the three row arms rather than once after the if-chain took the differing positions from 332 to 320, and the stored candidate has been updated to that shape. The jump count did not move, and the two extra jumps are located: both are in the movement block's arms, which jump forward to a join the compiler placed far away because the select branch sits between them, where the target falls straight through from the movement into the sound call at 137. Measured and inert: rewriting the chain with an explicit label and gotos, which is byte-identical to the if, else-if, else form because the compiler normalises it, so that is not a way to move the select branch. Measured and worse: storing the home x directly into D_8016D434 in both arms rather than computing it through a local first, which the target appears to do at 181 to 186, but which builds 329 positions against 320. The block placement is fixed and the jump count now matches. Writing the select branch as a trailing label that the three input paths goto, rather than as the else arm of the input chain, sinks it past the shared cell-lookup join exactly as the target does: the unconditional jump count goes from eleven to nine, which is the target's, and the join's sound call moves from index 159 to 147 against the target's 137. This is a trade and the numbers say so plainly. The correctly placed shape builds 378 of 382 with 321 differing positions, while the else-arm shape builds 380 with 320, so it scores worse on both of the counts that were being tracked while being structurally right. The stored candidate has been switched to the placed shape on the reasoning the jump-count lever gives, that placement is a property of the source and should be settled before register allocation. Also worth recording, because it looked like the same experiment: moving the join to a label and jumping to it from each arm is byte-identical to the plain chain, so it is specifically moving the select branch, not using a goto, that changes the layout. Two axes are now closed on the correctly placed shape rather than only on the earlier else-arm one, which matters because the profile sweep recorded before was against a structurally different candidate. Profiles: gcc_2_8_1_cc_g0_as_g8_split is identical to the default at 378 with 321, and gcc_2_8_1_g0_split_no_sched1, gcc_2_8_1_g0_no_sched2_split, gcc_2_8_1_g8_split and gcc_2_8_1_cc_g8_as_g0_split build 386, 374, 360 and 409 with 360, 375, 375 and 388 differing positions, so the profile axis is closed here too. The three-arm duplication of the D_8016D426 store is load bearing and should stay: reverting it to a single store after the row chain leaves the instruction count unchanged at 378 but raises the differing positions from 321 to 333. That also corrects a reading taken from the alignment during this pass, that the duplication was responsible for a ten-instruction excess around index 130. It is not; the alignment attributes those instructions there because the surrounding blocks are matched out of order, and the duplication costs nothing in length. The four instructions still missing are not in that block. Opcode distance is 26 against 321 differing positions, which puts a number on the reading recorded above that the position count badly overstates the damage. Twenty-six is the real size of the instruction-mix difference and it is where the missing four instructions live; the other three hundred positions are the order-sensitivity of the positional diff once a block moves. The opcode distance of 26 is now decomposed and localised. The candidate has five extra sll, two extra bne and one each of lbu, sb, sra and srl, and is missing five lui, three lb, two beq and one each of addiu, lhu, sh, addu and sltu. The three missing lb are the useful signal and they are all in the select branch. The target re-reads D_8016D401 and D_8016D402 from memory in the ordinary-key arm, at 280 and 285, where the build reuses the registers the cell lookup already loaded them into; and it re-reads D_8016D42C after the func_80168CDC call at 353, where the build keeps it in a callee-saved register across the call. So the residual is concentrated in that branch and it is common subexpression elimination working against the reconstruction rather than a shape error. Measured and inert: declaring D_8016D402 as s8 rather than casting a u8 at each use, which is byte-identical, so the earlier casts were never costing anything. Measured and worse: giving the ordinary-key arm its own locals for the two coordinate reads, which builds 379 with distance 27, so naming them does not defeat the elimination and costs an instruction. The opcode residual splits into two independent faults once nop is counted apart from sll. The larger is address materialisation: five missing lui and one missing addiu against five extra nop. That is the same signal that func_80168CDC turned out to have, where the target rematerialised a value at each use and the candidate hoisted it, leaving the delay slots empty. Five missing lui means five global addresses the target rebuilds and this candidate keeps in registers, which matches the standing observation that the target re-reads globals across the select branch. Try the late materialisation lever here before anything else; it is worth five nops and six arithmetic instructions, roughly half the distance of 26. The smaller fault is byte signedness. The struct field at +0x5E is signed, not unsigned. Declaring it s8 makes the lbu count exact at 12 against 12, takes the missing lb from 3 to 2, and moves the length from 378 to 380 against the target's 382. It is recorded as evidence rather than adopted because the total distance stays at 26: the two byte loads it fixes are paid for by an extra sll and sra sign-extension pair, so it needs the remaining two signed byte reads found before it pays. Measured and inert on this axis, individually and together: declaring D_8016D400, D_8016D402, D_8016D426 or D_8016ABC0 as s8 changes nothing at all, so the signedness question is about struct fields here and not about the globals. Note that measuring only the total distance hid this; the flips had to be scored on the lb and lbu counts alone to see that four of the five were inert and one was not. The address-materialisation half of the residual is now partly explained and partly closed, and the mechanism came from func_80180390's row rather than from this one. GCC 2.8.1 with -msplit-addresses hoists the high half of any global address read inside a loop the front end marks as a loop into a callee-saved register, and the target does not do that here. Writing the digit-walk as an explicit goto instead of a do/while removes the hoist, because GCC 2.8's loop optimiser only sees loops carrying loop notes. That takes the build from 378 instructions to the target's 382, so the length is now exact, and takes the missing lui count from five to three. The total opcode distance stays at 26 because the same change costs an sll and a subu elsewhere and moves one addu from matching to missing, which is why the lever has to be scored on the lui axis it targets rather than on the total. The three remaining missing lui are the select branch's reads of D_8016D401, D_8016D402 and D_8016AB38. On the select path those globals have not been read yet, so this is not a common subexpression across a join but the compiler hoisting the loads above the conditional so that one materialisation serves both paths, while the target materialises on each path separately. The stored candidate in notes/overlays/candidates.md is updated to the goto form, so the next pass starts at 382 with three rather than 378 with five. The signedness axis is now measured as a full cross product on the current goto-form base rather than one flip at a time, and it is closed. All thirty-two combinations of declaring the +0x5E field, D_8016D400, D_8016D402, D_8016D426 and D_8016ABC0 signed were built; every one reports opcode distance 26, unchanged. Scored on the byte axis rather than the total, the +0x5E field alone still halves it, taking lb from 11 to 12 against the target's 14 and lbu from 13 to exactly 12, but it costs two instructions and takes the length from the target's 382 to 384. That is why it is not adopted: the current candidate's exact instruction count is worth more than a two-point gain on one axis, and the earlier record of this trade was made against a shorter base where the count was not yet exact. The remaining branch-polarity difference is two beq in the target against two bne here, at target indices 252 and 255 where two consecutive beq compare the same register pair; that axis has not been swept and is the next thing to try. Improved from opcode distance 26 to 21, and the reason the earlier passes stalled is a struct layout error that neither headline metric could report. The widget's tail fields sit at +0x5E and +0x60, so the padding between +0x3E and them is 32 bytes, not 56; the stored candidate put them at +0x76 and +0x78, twenty-four bytes too far, and read the +0x60 field signed where the target reads it unsigned. The opcode distance cannot see that, because an sh is an sh at any offset, and the differing-position count could not either, because those positions already differed on their base register and so were counted before and after. The instruction multiset with the register fields masked out does see it, and it falls by fourteen. That measure is now worth running across every stored candidate rather than only on the one being worked, which is how this was found: an audit of all five reported this function's +0x76 and +0x78 against the target's +0x5E and +0x60 immediately. Three source shapes follow from reading the columns after that. The frame counter's test drops its (s16) cast, worth two of the distance. The cursor's forward wrap compares == 15 rather than >= 15, worth one. The cell lookup takes the table entry whole rather than masking it with 0xF, worth two more, and the mask was never in the target. Measured and inert: the signedness of the byte globals and whether their casts are written, because combine turns a cast of an unsigned byte load into lb either way; and spelling the cell lookup as a two-dimensional index, a flat signed index or a flat unsigned one, all byte-identical. Note that the differing-position count moves the wrong way across this work, 311 to 352, because removing instructions displaces everything after them; the distance and the register-blind measure both improve, and they are the ones to believe here. Residual is now two branch polarities, three signed byte loads against one unsigned, two lui, and a shift pair against an add pair. Arity audit (tools/project/overlay_arity_audit.py) reported that the stored candidate does not make the target's last two calls, to NameEntry_AdjustLength at 0x8016909C and SD_SEPlayFull at 0x8003FEE0. Reading the source against that report exposed a real fault: both NameEntry_AdjustLength sites always play a sound, and the target selects a0 = 12 over a0 = 9 with bnez before falling into one jal, so the shape is SD_SEPlayFull(NameEntry_AdjustLength(...) ? 12 : 9) and not if (NameEntry_AdjustLength(...) == 0) SD_SEPlayFull(9). The candidate had dropped the 12 path at both sites. Correcting both took the candidate from 377 instructions and opcode distance 21 to 380 and 18, and the two corrections compose: either alone gives 20 or 19. Sixteen ternary spellings and all 29 profiles are flat at 18. The call placement difference survives the fix and is a separate open fault: the target lays that block out after the main body jumps to the epilogue at index 358, while the candidate emits it inline at the select gate, and a forward goto to the end of the function measures worse at 19. An earlier reading of the same audit output recorded six per-site argument shortfalls here; those were artefacts of pairing call sites by ordinal across streams of different length. Shift-form audit against the target: the target has 20 sll, 5 sra and 1 sllv, and the stored candidate has 20 sll, 6 sra, 1 srl and 1 sllv. So the candidate emits one sra and one srl that the target does not, which is two of its two extra instructions and is a content difference rather than a scheduling one. An extra sra usually means a signed value where the target has an unsigned one, or a sign extension the target does not perform; the srl has no counterpart at all. Both are worth resolving before any further order work, and neither is visible in the opcode distance, which counts sra and srl as separate classes but does not say which side is over. Taken from opcode distance 18 to 15 by two content fixes read off the target's opcode classes rather than its positions, and both are about where a value is written rather than what the code says. First the frame countdown is a u16 local: the target stores the raw decremented value with sh and then tests it with sll v0,v0,0x10 followed by bnez, which is how GCC asks whether the low sixteen bits are non-zero, while an s32 local tests all thirty-two and needs no shift. Second the 0x4000 flag is masked into a local before it is tested: written as flag = (D_8009B3A4[0] & 0x4000) != 0 the compiler recognises a single-bit test and folds it to srl by fourteen and andi by one, which is where the candidate's spare srl came from, while the target has andi by 0x4000 followed by sltu s0,zero,v0, the form a comparison against a value it cannot see as one bit produces. Naming the masked value defeats the fold and supplies the sltu. A third fault is decoded and confirmed but not yet adoptable: the first cursor wrap is >= 15 and not == 15. The target has slti v0,v0,15 followed by bnez past the body, so the body runs when the value is at least fifteen; == compiles to a bne against a materialised 15. Spelling it >= supplies the missing slti exactly, but costs three extra nops as load-delay stalls, so it measures two worse and is left out of the stored candidate until something fills those slots. Also measured on this base and not helping: f5E as s16 or u16, f3C as s16, D_8016D400 and D_8016D426 as u16, D_8016D402 and D_8016D426 as s8, both tables as flat one-dimensional arrays with the row arithmetic written out, and four spellings of the countdown test including an explicit (u16) cast and a mask. What remains in the mix is lui twice and addu once against addiu twice, which is an addressing form; lb twice and lh once against one sra, which is signed narrow loads; one sh against one sb; one spare subu; and two nops. Taken from opcode distance 15 to 14 and to the target's exact instruction count of 382. The change is a single subtraction written the other way round. The target computes the tween distance with addu, so the constant 16 is subtracted from the widget's current position and the result added, rather than 16 being folded into a home value that is then subtracted. Writing home = 16 - w->f3C followed by delta = w->f5E + home supplies the addu, removes one subu and takes the count from 381 to 382. The flat form, delta = w->f5E - w->f3C + 16, reaches the same count but measures 16, and negating the difference is byte-identical to the original, so the improvement is specifically about which operand carries the constant rather than about associativity. The frame countdown is then cheapest as an s32 local with the test cast, if ((u16)n != 0), worth one differing position over the u16 local and identical on every other measure. Re-measured on this base and inert: D_8016D402, D_8016D426, D_8016D400 and D_8016ABC0 declared signed, all sixteen combinations, so the two lb the target has over this build are not reachable by declaring a byte global signed; four spellings of the countdown test crossed with three spellings of the first cursor wrap and both widths of D_8016D4D4, twenty-four cells; routing either of the two early returns through a shared label at the end of the function, which is completely inert here although it was worth seven on func_80180390; and all 29 profiles, with only gcc_2_8_1_cc_g0_as_g8_split tying the default. The >= 15 wrap remains confirmed from the target's slti and remains too expensive to adopt. What is left in the mix is two lui against two addiu, one sh against one sb, two lb and one lh against one sra, one spare subu, the slti, and two nops. Taken from opcode distance 14 to 11 by two findings read off the narrow load and store widths rather than off the positions, and they compose: 12 and 13 alone, 11 together. First, the cursor's x position is stored straight into D_8016D434 in both arms of the eleventh-column test rather than computed into a local and stored once; the target has two sh to that address and this build had one, which is what a local produces. Second, the y position is stored before func_800429D8 rather than after it; the target reloads both D_8016D434 and D_8016D436 with lh when it computes the two tween deltas, and this build reloaded only the first, because the second store sat after the call and GCC could still see the stored value in a register, so moving the store above the call makes the call clobber it and forces the reload. Both are the same observation from two directions: the target keeps these two globals in memory rather than in registers across this block. The method that found them is worth repeating: comparing the per-opcode counts of lb, lh, lbu, lhu, sb and sh with the immediate offsets attached, so that a missing lh is attributable to a named address rather than merely counted. Re-measured on this base and closed: all sixty-four combinations of the widget struct's field widths across f30/f32, f36/f38, f3C, f5E and f60, none better than 14 before these two changes; all sixteen combinations of D_8016D402, D_8016D426, D_8016D400 and D_8016ABC0 declared signed, completely flat, so the two lb the target still has over this build are not reachable that way; and three spellings of the first cursor wrap crossed with two of the lower bound and two of the D_8016D42C read, where >= 15 still costs two despite being confirmed from the target's slti. Reading D_8016D42C into a local instead of twice is a false economy: it reaches 379 instructions and the same distance, but the target reads that address twice with lb at indices 333 and 353, so the two reads are correct. What is left in the mix is two lui against two addiu, two lb against one sra and one sb, the slti, one spare subu and one nop. Taken from opcode distance 11 to 10 and back to the target's exact 382 instructions by writing the last cursor-column scale as a multiplication rather than a shift. (D_8016D42C << 4) + 112 and D_8016D42C * 16 + 112 are the same value and different code: the shift form makes GCC load the s8 with lbu and then sign-extend and scale together, sll by 24 followed by sra by 20, which is three instructions, while the multiplication form loads with lb, already sign-extended, and scales with a single sll by 4. The target has the lb, so the source multiplies. Assigning the global to a local before the expression reaches the same place, which is the same effect by another route, and declaring D_8016D42C s16 or s32 is worth four in the wrong direction. The method matters as much as the result: this was found by aligning the sequences of lb, lbu and sra on both sides with difflib instead of comparing their totals. The totals reported two lb missing and one sra extra, which reads as three separate problems; the alignment showed a single replacement at the very end of the function and named the statement responsible. Re-measured on this base and still best as they stand: the tween distance as home = 16 - w->f3C with an addition, where reverting to the subtraction form costs one and three other spellings cost one to two, so the earlier finding survives the two intervening base changes; and the first cursor wrap as == 15, where >= 15 still costs two despite being confirmed from the target's slti. What is left in the mix is two lui and one lbu and one lb on the target side against two addiu, one subu, one nop and one sb on this build's, and the missing lui are the last two in the function, so the remaining addressing difference is at the tail rather than spread through it. The cost of the confirmed >= 15 wrap is now itemised rather than quoted as a number, which turns it into a narrow question. Against this base the eq spelling leaves a mix difference of two lui, one lbu, one slti and one lb on the target side against two addiu, one subu, one nop and one sb. Switching to >= removes the slti from that list, exactly as predicted, and in exchange the nop count goes from one to four and one addiu becomes a third missing lui: the totals become three lui, one lbu and one lb against one addiu, one subu, four nop and one sb, so 10 becomes 12 and the count goes from 382 to 384. The whole penalty is three load-delay stalls. So >= is not wrong and is not expensive in itself; it reorders the cursor-increment block into a shape where the scheduler has nothing independent to move into three delay slots. The next question is what supplies that work, not whether the comparison is signed. Also measured on this base and closed: all eight combinations of declaring the three volatile pad words as scalars rather than one-element arrays, which are byte-identical because GCC already addresses x[0] on an extern array exactly as it addresses a scalar, so that is not where the two addiu come from; nine combinations of the two dispatch tables as two-dimensional arrays, flat arrays with the row arithmetic written out, and pointers, where every non-pointer cell is distance 10 and both pointer cells are 17; and an eighteen-cell product of three tween-distance spellings against two countdown tests against three wrap comparisons, whose best cell is the current shape. The spare subu is located. Aligning the addu and subu sequences with their instruction indices shows the target holding two addu at 153 and 156 where this build has one subu at 170, and disassembling both sides explains it. In the cell-walk loop the target keeps row * 15 in a1 and the table base in a3 across the whole loop and re-adds them each iteration, so its body is addu, sll, sra, addu, addu, sb, lb. This build recomputes the row offset inside the loop with sll by 4 followed by subu, so its body is one instruction longer and carries the extra subu. The target has hoisted a loop-invariant that this build recomputes. Nine shapes were measured against that and none of them both hoists and keeps the count. A row pointer taken once before the loop hoists but reaches 377 instructions and distance 11; a flat array with the row offset in a named local reaches 377 and 15; the flat array with the arithmetic written out at each site is 382 and 10, one differing position better than the current shape but otherwise identical. The three structured loop forms, do-while, while and for, all hoist and all reach 378 and 12, which is four instructions short rather than one long, so they remove more than the hoist is worth. A goto with the test at the top is 380 and 14. Splitting row and col into separate locals for the loop and for the later lookup, crossed with the goto and do-while forms, moves nothing. So the hoist is real and reachable, but every spelling that produces it also removes instructions the target keeps, and the open question is which shape hoists the row offset without also folding the two adds that follow it. Four more axes closed on this base and one methodological limit recorded. Dropping volatile from each of the three pad words in all eight combinations is never better: removing it from D_8009B398 alone is byte-identical, so that one is not load-bearing here, while removing it from D_8009B3A4 costs four and removing two costs six. A 32-cell product of the loop form against the cursor wrap against the tween-distance spelling against the countdown test against the table indexing has its best cell at the current shape; the flat table form ties on distance with one fewer differing position but changes the declaration away from the two-dimensional shape the row stride of 15 supports, so it is not adopted. A 116-cell product of all 29 profiles against the four leading shapes moves nothing, with only gcc_2_8_1_cc_g0_as_g8_split tying the default. The limit is worth recording because it cost time: the sequence-alignment technique that located the sra, the subu and both of func_80180390's faults does not apply to this function's narrow accesses, because every one of them is to a relocated scalar global and so the candidate side of the alignment is a row of zero immediates carrying no information. It works where the operands are structural, such as struct member offsets, and is noise where they are %lo relocations. The general form of that is now in notes/overlays/README.md.

name: NameEntry_UpdateDialog

This is the password screen's message box driver, keyed on the u16 D_8016D4D2 holding a message id in the low twelve bits with flags 0x8000 and 0x4000 above it, and on the flag byte D_8016D400. name: func_8016A080
notes: Exact boundary from the verified overlay split. Builds the password entry screen. It clears the eight bytes at D_8016D410 from the top down and the fields at D_8016D424 and D_8016D428 then calls Password_RefreshDigitDisplay Password_RefreshStarchipDisplay and Password_CreateMessageBox with 226 and 1. It loads the screen background through func_80029574 with D_800EA0E8 keeping it in D_8016D430 and sizing it 320 by 256 and 512 by 240 through the four halfwords at +0x28. It then creates the entry field as a type 2 object at 152 by 40 with widths 2 and 3 depth -8 and flag 0x8 and hands it to func_8016A02C with 1; then a type 1 object at 256 by 120 sized 32 by 32 with 13 in both halfwords at +0x48 whose flag word at +4 loses bit 0x08000000 and gains 0x50000000 before func_80042918 depth 10 hook func_80169E20 and Password_SetDigitCursorTarget - its +0x30 copies its own +0x18 and it is kept in D_8016D420. Finally four type 2 objects are created one per password digit through func_80040468 with 3 1 the index 11 and 524 each gaining bit 0x40000000 depth 8 hook Password_UpdateDigitCursorDecoration and flags 0x28 and stored in D_8016D440; the screen ends with func_8003FF08 of 29520 and func_80015A00. Builds 161 of 161 instructions with 72 differing positions. Lever found: the D_8016D424 and D_8016D428 clears must precede the byte loop not follow it - after the loop the body builds 160 which is one short. Measured and not helping: writing the four background size stores through a local copy of D_8016D430 instead of the global which builds 160; sharing the loop counter with the fourth argument of func_800404CC which also builds 160 even though the target passes a register there rather than zero; an explicit walking pointer for the clear loop which builds 161 with 75 differences; a do-while form; an explicit array size; and pointer syntax for the index. What remains is that the target strength-reduces the clear loop into a walking pointer initialised as base plus 7 and decremented in the branch delay slot while the build recomputes base plus index every iteration. Retested after #787 added a strength-reduce axis: the profile is not suppressing anything. Compiling the clear loop alone with and without -fno-strength-reduce under gcc_2_8_1_g0_split gives byte-identical assembly so the pass is not firing on this loop either way and the reduced form in the target has to come from the source. Probing eight loop spellings directly through the compiler rather than through full overlay builds found it: i equals 7 then p equals the array plus i as its own statement then a for with an empty first clause decrementing both. That reproduces the target exactly including addu of base and the counter register rather than the folded relocation. Writing the pointer as address-of element 7 or as array plus 7 folds the offset into %hi and %lo of symbol plus 7 which the target does not have; indexing the array inside the loop leaves the add inside the loop. With that loop and the four background size stores written through the global the body now builds 161 of 161 with 56 differing positions down from 72. What remains starts at the background pointer: the target stores the func_80029574 result into D_8016D430 in the call's delay slot and then reloads it with lw before the four size stores while every source form tried so far keeps the returned value in a register instead. The background pointer residual is solved: D_8016D430 is volatile. The target stores the func_80029574 result into it in the call's delay slot and then reloads it with lw into a different register before the four size stores, and a probe reproduces that only with the qualifier - plain, through a local copy, and with the global spelled at each store all give byte-identical code that keeps the returned value in a register and never reloads. The probe output matches the target instruction for instruction including which register takes the reload and which takes the constants. This was found by extending tools/project/overlay_scan_reloads.py, which previously could not see this case because it treats any store as a legitimate reason to reload and clears its record. Correction: D_8016D430 is not volatile and the conclusion recorded above is wrong. The reload has an ordinary explanation. The assignment stores D_800EA0E8 into the global and func_80029574 is called after it, so the call invalidates memory and the following read has to reload. The probe that concluded volatile put the store after the call instead of before it, which removed the invalidation and left the qualifier as the only thing that could produce a reload. Worse, volatile is actively wrong here: it stops the store being moved into the call's delay slot, which is where the target has it, so the qualified form spends a nop there. Written unqualified as D_8016D430 = D_800EA0E8 then the call then a local read, the background block matches instruction for instruction. Reconstructed from this note the function now builds 160 of 161 with 73 differing positions and is exact through instruction 90. The one missing instruction is the flag word at plus 4, which the target stores twice, once after clearing bit 0x08000000 and once after setting 0x50000000. Every form tried collapses the two into a single store: two separate compound assignments, an explicit local carrying the value across both, and the two halfword stores at plus 0x48 and plus 0x4A interleaved between them to break up the combination. Now 161 of 161 with nine differing positions, down from the recorded 56, and all nine are register naming rather than instruction differences. Three findings. The flag word at plus 4 is stored twice because the first store is volatile and the second is not. GCC eliminates a first store to the same location in every plain form - seven were measured, including two compound assignments, an explicit local carried across both, recomputing the second value from the original rather than from the first, and interleaving the two halfword stores between them - so something has to defeat dead store elimination. Qualifying both stores does give two stores but costs a nop, because a volatile store cannot be moved into the call's delay slot where the target has the second one. Qualifying only the first gives both effects at once. The general form is worth keeping: use volatile to keep a store that would otherwise be dead, but never on the store that has to fill a delay slot. Second, the loop counter's zero must be assigned just before its first use rather than earlier; assigned early, GCC reuses that register for the unrelated literal zero argument to func_80029574 where the target uses the zero register, which was worth three positions. Third, naming the digit hook Password_UpdateDigitCursorDecoration in a local before the slot pointer rather than spelling it inside the loop swaps s2 and s3 the right way round, worth two more. The remaining nine are the v0 and v1 pairing through the flag block. The remaining nine positions are robust and are a register allocation tie-break rather than a shape. The flag value takes v1 in the build where the target uses v0, and the two constants take the other register, with the instructions otherwise identical. Measured and not helping: reading the flag word before the two halfword stores rather than after; splitting the read from the mask so the read is the first statement of the block; naming the 0x50000000 constant in a local; naming the 13 constant in a local; and qualifying the read volatile as well as the first store. The flag value has much the longer live range and should win the lower register on priority, so whatever decides it is not visible in the source. The nine-position residual reproduces in a twelve-line probe of the flag block alone, which is the most useful thing to record about it: the cluster is intrinsic to that block rather than imported from the rest of the function, so it can be worked at probe cost instead of rebuilding all 161 instructions. The probe shows exactly what decides the pairing. Re-reading the flag word for the second store gives the target's pairing, the value in v0 and the constants in v1, but costs an extra lw, because the volatile first store defeats the common subexpression and forces a real reload. Reusing the masked value from a local gives the target's instruction count and sequence but swaps the pair. Eight reuse spellings were measured and every one is byte-identical: an extra copy local between the two stores, naming the 13 in a local, naming the 0x50000000 in a local, hoisting the read above the two halfword stores, splitting the read from the mask, declaring the value signed, changing declaration order, and moving the halfword stores after the mask. Holding the object in a callee-saved register by taking it from a call, which mirrors the real function where it lives in s0 across two calls, is also inert, so the swap is not an artefact of the probe's simpler context. On the profile axis, gcc_2_8_1_g0_no_sched2_split, gcc_2_8_1_g8_split and gcc_2_8_1_g0_keep_large_ori are identical to the default. gcc_2_8_1_g0_split_no_sched1 does produce the target's v0 and v1 pairing, but it is not the answer: it reorders the block so the mask constant is materialised into v1 before the load rather than into a1, and the target keeps the mask in a1 across the move of the object into a0. So the pairing is now closed against source shape and against the profile knob, and the next idea has to come from somewhere other than this block's spelling. Rebuilt and the 161 of 161 with nine differing positions is now stored in notes/overlays/candidates.md and re-verified from the stored copy. Two details that decide the count were not stated clearly enough to reproduce from. The clear loop has to be a do-while with the test at the bottom, which is what the target's store, decrement, bgez, decrement-in-delay shape is; writing it as an unconditional for with a break at the end is semantically the same but peels the first iteration and builds 162 with 154 differing positions. And func_80029574 takes one argument, not two: the target never sets a1, and the D_800EA0E8 address is materialised only for the store into D_8016D430. Passing it as a second argument costs three positions, 12 against 9. The recorded lever about assigning the loop counter's zero just before its first use is confirmed and is worth three more, 15 against 12. Applying the jump-count lever: target and candidate both have zero unconditional jumps, so block placement is already right and the nine remaining positions are register allocation, which agrees with the earlier finding that they are closed against source and profile. Opcode distance is zero, so the nine differing positions are entirely register choice and scheduling. With the jump counts also equal, both structural axes are closed and only the allocator's pairing remains.

Unblocked by the resident match of func_8002D458, which established the .rodata subsegment route for a compiler-emitted jump table, and the route is now verified for this function rather than assumed. A probe of just the guards and the dispatch, compiled with gcc_2_8_1_g0_split, emits a .rodata of exactly 0x14 bytes, five words, which is the size of jtbl_8016807C, and reproduces the target's dispatch instruction for instruction: andi with 0x1f, sltiu against 5, beqz to the default, then sll by 2, addu, lw and jr through the table. Source shapes confirmed by that probe: the state is state = D_8016D424 & 0x1F with a plain switch over cases 0 to 4 and no default body, since the compiler's own range check is what produces the early return; the widget guard is a test of bit 0x40 of +0x6C on D_8016D420; and the second guard must be written as a comparison against 0x2000 rather than as a truth test, because that is what emits li v1 8192 followed by bne. Case entry points are indices 32, 145, 196, 262 and 329, and the shared return is index 359. Case 0 opens by testing D_8009B3A4 against 0xA000 for left and right, stepping D_8016D428 up with a clamp at 7 or down with a clamp at 0, then playing sound 47 through func_8003FEE0, calling func_8016A00C with the widget, storing 8 into the widget's +0x60 and setting bit 0x40 of its +0x6C; when 0xA000 is clear it falls to a test of D_8009B394 against 0x5000 for up and down at index 71. The whole function is now decoded and written. All five cases, the dispatch and the shared tail are mapped, and the first full candidate builds 366 instructions against 365, so the structure is close from the start. Four source shapes are established by measurement. The three pad globals must be declared the way main_menu already declares them, extern volatile u16 X[] read through index 0: the target reads each of D_8009B3A4, D_8009B394 and D_8009B398 twice, and without volatile the compiler folds each pair into one load, which is structurally wrong even though it is shorter. The result of func_8016A304 must be assigned straight into D_8016D4DC rather than through a local, because a local costs a move before the store. func_80021894 takes D_8016D4DC as an argument rather than none; that single correction took the differing positions from 358 to 145, which is the largest single improvement found for this function and is why the argument list is worth reading off the delay slots rather than assumed. Case 1 falls through into case 2 with no break, ending with a store of 2 into D_8016D424 and continuing into case 2's body. Case 3 steps a counter down by a cascade whose divisors are 10, 20, 30 and 40 under guards of 10, 100, 1000 and 10000, with a final step of 1 when the division yields zero. The f21 byte of D_8016D4D8 is read unsigned in case 1, where the target uses lbu against zero, and signed in case 4, where it uses lb against zero, so the member is u8 with an s8 cast at the case 4 test.
